# Seasonal stellar visibility {#sec-stellar}

The default uses Schaefer's directional twilight brightness and Hecht's naked-eye point-source threshold for heliacal rising (first morning visibility) and acronycal setting (last evening visibility). On each local mean-solar date the calculation searches the terrain-clear rising branch before noon and descending branch after noon, with the Sun below the astronomical horizon. A transition marks the first qualifying morning following an unsuccessful morning, or the last qualifying evening preceding an unsuccessful evening. Solar altitude, stellar zenith distance and the difference in azimuth determine the twilight background. The limiting magnitude sets the dark zenith reference. Rozenberg airmass and the extinction coefficient attenuate the star. Stellar clearance and extinction use the selected apparent or geometric altitude. Solar altitude in the twilight equation is geometric.

The passage bands, phase type, heliacal setting and acronycal rising use Purrington's altitude-difference rule on a 365-sample solar-longitude cycle. The `solar.alt` cutoff and `alt.rs` passage ceiling apply to this classification. Therefore a Schaefer event marker may lie inside a passage band. Selecting the Purrington method also derives first morning and last evening from the passage transitions. A horizon object must cover all bearings. With coordinates, alt.hor supplies the constant skyline.

The Schaefer fit was developed for twilight near the horizon. Searches at high latitudes or far from the solar azimuth can extend outside its empirical range. The calculation assumes a clear sky and a fixed observer limit. Moonlight, weather and observer adaptation can affect field sightings. Treat an integrated cluster magnitude as a single unresolved target.

Use `metadata$events$date.julian` for a dated reconstruction. It gives the local Julian-calendar date. The month labels on the plot divide solar longitude into twelve equal sectors.

[Accuracy against observed dates](heliacal-rising.qmd#v01-observations).

## How the visibility threshold is calculated

For each terrain-clear point on the star’s track, let $h_\odot$ be the geometric solar altitude, $z$ the stellar zenith distance and $\Delta A$ the unsigned difference in azimuth, all in radians. Schaefer’s twilight term at the star is

$$
\log_{10} B_t=4.75-\Delta A z/3+h_\odot(12+8.21z)+2.86z.
$$

For extinction $k$ in magnitudes per airmass the package evaluates the threshold at background $B=B_0+(k/0.2)\max(0,B_t-118)$ in nanolamberts. It obtains the dark background $B_0$ by inverting the Hecht threshold at the observer’s zenith limiting magnitude plus $k$. The stellar magnitude at altitude $h$ is $m+kX(h)$, where $X$ is Rozenberg’s airmass. A sample qualifies when that magnitude is at least as bright as the threshold. A larger azimuth separation from the Sun can therefore make a star detectable at a different solar depression even at the same altitude. The fitted twilight domain was approximately −18° to −6° solar altitude, stellar zenith distance above 60° and azimuth difference below 90°. [Schaefer’s twilight equations and reference calculations](https://doi.org/10.1177/002182868701801103).

The passage calculation uses a vertical star–Sun separation of $2.1m+10$ degrees, with catalogue magnitude $m$, together with extinction, solar altitude and terrain clearance. The low-altitude rising and descending opportunities determine the R, S and RS bands. I denotes no visibility under this rule and V denotes visibility without a classified rising or setting passage. A star can clear the skyline throughout the year and still change seasonal class.

## Comparing the same season across stars and epochs {#phase-comparisons}

[`plot.skyscapeR.starphases()`](fn-plot-skyscaper-starphases.html) places a result and any further results on a common seasonal axis beginning at December solstice. A single cycle can be drawn as a ring or a strip. Multiple results occupy concentric rings from the outside inward, or aligned strips in the linear layout. The month divisions are a shared seasonal reference. Use the saved event date for a historical calendar comparison. Ordering results by star or epoch and holding the skyline and visibility thresholds fixed makes it possible to attribute changes in the boundaries to the chosen comparison. The plot reads the classifications already calculated by [`star.phases()`](fn-star-phases.html). Adding a ring does not refit the visibility model.
